hook.text: A hurricane starts as a whisper — warm, moist air rising off tropical ocean water above 26°C.

buildup.text: As the air rises, it cools and releases energy. Surrounding air rushes in and starts to spin.

discovery.text: Earth's rotation bends the wind into a spiral. A calm eye forms at the center of the storm.

twist.text: The eye feels peaceful — clear skies and light wind — but the worst winds surround it.

climax.text: A single hurricane releases the energy of 10,000 nuclear bombs over its lifetime.

punchline.text: The most destructive storms on Earth start with nothing but warm water and air.

quiz.question: What minimum ocean temperature is needed for a hurricane to form?

details.summary: Hurricanes form over warm tropical oceans when sea surface temperatures exceed 26 degrees Celsius, providing energy for convective storms to organize into a rotating low-pressure system. The Coriolis effect sets the system spinning, and warm moist air spiraling inward fuels intensification.
details.whyItMatters: Warming oceans are expanding the regions where hurricanes can form and intensify. Understanding formation explains why climate change makes the most powerful storms even more destructive.
takeaways: Sea surface temperatures above 26 degrees Celsius fuel hurricane formation
The Coriolis effect causes the characteristic spiral rotation
Low wind shear allows the storm structure to build vertically

faq.question: Why don't hurricanes form at the equator?
faq.answer: The Coriolis effect is zero at the equator and too weak within about 5 degrees latitude. Without sufficient rotational deflection, storms cannot organize into the spiral structure needed to sustain a hurricane.

faq.question: Is climate change creating more hurricanes?
faq.answer: The total number of hurricanes may not increase, but the proportion of the most intense Category 4 and 5 storms is rising. Warmer oceans provide more energy, and storms are intensifying faster and producing heavier rainfall.
